section.heading: 16.6. Parametric Surfaces and Their Areas
section.paragraph: So far we have considered special types of surfaces: cylinders, quadric surfaces, graphs of functions of two variables, and level surfaces of functions of three variables. Here we use vector functions to describe more general surfaces, called parametric surfaces, and compute their areas. Then we take the general surface area formula and see how it applies to special surfaces.
section.heading: Parametric Surfaces
section.paragraph: In much the same way that we describe a space curve by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ of a single parameter $$t$$ , we can describe a surface by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ of two parameters $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ . We suppose that
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

is a vector-valued function defined on a region $$D$$ in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane. So $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , the component functions of $$\mathbf{r}$$ , are functions of the two variables $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ with domain $$D$$ . The set of all points $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ such that
$${x = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)} {y = y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)} {z = z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)}$$

and $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ varies throughout $$D$$ , is called a parametric surface $$S$$ and Equations 2 are called parametric equations of $$S$$ . Each choice of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ gives a point on $$S$$ ; by making all choices, we get all of $$S$$ . In other words, the surface $$S$$ is traced out by the tip of the position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ as $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ moves throughout the region $$D$$ . (See Figure 1.)

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Identify and sketch the surface with vector equation
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = 2\cos u\mathbf{i} + \upsilon\mathbf{j} + 2\sin u\mathbf{k}$$
Solution The parametric equations for this surface are
$${x = 2\cos u} {y = \upsilon} {z = 2\sin u}$$
So for any point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on the surface, we have

This means that vertical cross-sections parallel to the $$xz$$ -plane (that is, with $$y$$ constant) are all circles with radius $$2$$ . Since $$y = \upsilon$$ and no restriction is placed on $$\upsilon$$ , the surface is a circular cylinder with radius $$2$$ whose axis is the $$y$$ -axis (see Figure 2).

section.paragraph: In Example 1 we placed no restrictions on the parameters $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ and so we obtained the entire cylinder. If, for instance, we restrict $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ by writing the parameter domain as
$${0 \leqslant u \leqslant \pi \slash 2} {0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 3}$$
then $$x \geqslant 0$$ , $$z \geqslant 0$$ , $$0 \leqslant y \leqslant 3$$ , and we get the quarter-cylinder with length $$3$$ illustrated in Figure 3.

section.paragraph: If a parametric surface $$S$$ is given by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ , then there are two useful families of curves that lie on $$S$$ , one family with $$u$$ constant and the other with $$\upsilon$$ constant. These families correspond to vertical and horizontal lines in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane. If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 4.)

Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ . We call these curves grid curves. (In Example 1, for instance, the grid curves obtained by letting $$u$$ be constant are horizontal lines, whereas the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are circles.) In fact, when a computer graphs a parametric surface, it sometimes depicts the surface by plotting these grid curves, as we will see in the following example.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Use a computer to graph the surface
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = {\langle{\left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\cos u,\left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\sin u,u + \cos\upsilon}\rangle}$$
Which grid curves have $$u$$ constant? Which have $$\upsilon$$ constant?

Solution We graph the portion of the surface with parameter domain $$0 \leqslant u \leqslant 4\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 2\pi$$ in Figure 5. It has the appearance of a spiral tube. To identify the grid curves, we write the corresponding parametric equations:
$${x = \left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\cos u} {y = \left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\sin u} {z = u + \cos\upsilon}$$

If $$\upsilon$$ is constant, then $$\sin\upsilon$$ and $$\cos\upsilon$$ are constant, so the parametric equations resemble those of the helix in Example 13.1.4. Thus the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are the spiral curves in Figure 5. We deduce that the grid curves with $$u$$ constant must be the curves that look like circles in the figure. Further evidence for this assertion is that if $$u$$ is kept constant, $$u = u_{0}$$ , then the equation $$z = u_{0} + \cos\upsilon$$ shows that the $$z$$ -values vary from $$u_{0} - 1$$ to $$u_{0} + 1$$ .

section.paragraph: In Examples 1 and 2 we were given a vector equation and asked to graph the corresponding parametric surface. In the following examples, however, we are given the more challenging problem of finding a vector function to represent a given surface. In the rest of this chapter we will often need to do exactly that.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find a vector function that represents the plane that passes through the point $$P_{0}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}_{0}$$ and that contains two nonparallel vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

Solution If $$P$$ is any point in the plane, we can get from $$P_{0}$$ to $$P$$ by moving a certain distance in the direction of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and another distance in the direction of $$\mathbf{b}$$ . So there are scalars $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ such that $$\overset{\rightarrow}{P_{0}P} = u\mathbf{a} + v\mathbf{b}$$ . (Figure 6 illustrates how this works, by means of the Parallelogram Law, for the case where $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are positive. See also Exercise 12.2.46.) If $$\mathbf{r}$$ is the position vector of $$P$$ , then
$$\mathbf{r} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OP_{0}} + \overset{\rightarrow}{P_{0}P} = \mathbf{r}_{0} + u\mathbf{a} + \upsilon\mathbf{b}$$
So the vector equation of the plane can be written as
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = \mathbf{r}_{0} + u\mathbf{a} + \upsilon\mathbf{b}$$
where $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are real numbers.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation of the sphere

Solution The sphere has a simple representation $$\rho = a$$ in spherical coordinates, so let’s choose the angles $$\phi$$ and $$\theta$$ in spherical coordinates as the parameters (see Section 15.8). Then, putting $$\rho = a$$ in the equations for conversion from spherical to rectangular coordinates (Equations 15.8.1), we obtain
$$x = {a\sin\phi\cos\theta} y = {a\sin\phi\sin\theta} z = {a\cos\phi}$$
as the parametric equations of the sphere. The corresponding vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = a\sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a\sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a\cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$

We have $$0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi$$ and $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , so the parameter domain is the rectangle $$D = \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . The grid curves with $$\phi$$ constant are the circles of constant latitude (including the equator). The grid curves with $$\theta$$ constant are the meridians (semicircles), which connect the north and south poles (see Figure 7).

section.paragraph: Note We saw in Example 4 that the grid curves for a sphere are curves of constant latitude or constant longitude. For a general parametric surface we are really making a map and the grid curves are similar to lines of latitude and longitude. Describing a point on a parametric surface (like the one in Figure 5) by giving specific values of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ is like giving the latitude and longitude of a point.

One of the uses of parametric surfaces is in computer graphics. Figure 8 shows the result of trying to graph the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ by solving the equation for $$z$$ and graphing the top and bottom hemispheres separately. Part of the sphere appears to be missing because of the rectangular grid system used by the software. The much better picture in Figure 9 was produced by a computer using the parametric equations found in Example 4.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation for the cylinder
$${x^{2} + y^{2} = 4} {0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1}$$

Solution The cylinder has a simple representation $$r = 2$$ in cylindrical coordinates, so we choose as parameters $$\theta$$ and $$z$$ in cylindrical coordinates. Then the parametric equations of the cylinder are
$$x = {2\cos\theta} y = {2\sin\theta} z = z$$
where $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ and $$0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1$$ . In vector notation,
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\theta,z} \right) = 2\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + 2\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + z\mathbf{k}$$
and the vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ maps the parameter domain
$$D = \left\{ (\theta,z) \middle| 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi,0 \leq z \leq 1 \right\}$$
to a cylinder, as shown in Figure 10

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find a vector function that represents the elliptic paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ .
Solution If we regard $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters, then the parametric equations are simply
and the vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {x,y} \right) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + {({x^{2} + 2y^{2}})}^{}\mathbf{k}$$

section.paragraph: In general, a surface given as the graph of a function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , that is, with an equation of the form $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , can always be regarded as a parametric surface by taking $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters and writing the parametric equations as
$$x = x y = y z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$
In Module 16.6 you can investigate several families of parametric surfaces.
Parametric representations (also called parametrizations) of surfaces are not unique. The next example shows two ways to parametrize a cone.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation for the surface $$z = 2\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ , that is, the top half of the cone $$z^{2} = 4x^{2} + 4y^{2}$$ .
Solution 1 One possible representation is obtained by choosing $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters:
So the vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {x,y} \right) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\mathbf{k}$$

Solution 2 Another representation results from choosing as parameters the polar coordinates $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ . A point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on the cone satisfies $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , and $$z = 2\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = 2r$$ . So a vector equation for the cone is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {r,\theta} \right) = r\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + r\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + 2r\mathbf{k}$$
where $$r \geqslant 0$$ and $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .

For some purposes the parametric representations in Solutions 1 and 2 of Example 7 are equally good, but Solution 2 might be preferable in certain situations. If we are interested only in the part of the cone that lies below the plane $$z = 1$$ , for instance, all we have to do in Solution 2 is change the parameter domain to
$$D = \left\{ (r,\theta)|0 \leq r \leq \frac{1}{2},0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}$$
Then the vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ maps the region $$D$$ to the half-cone shown in Figure 11.

section.heading: Surfaces of Revolution
section.paragraph: Surfaces of revolution can be represented parametrically. For instance, let’s consider the surface $$S$$ obtained by rotating the curve $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis, where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ . Let $$\theta$$ be the angle of rotation as shown in Figure 12. If $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is a point on $$S$$ , then
$$x = x y = f(x)\cos\theta z = f(x)\sin\theta$$

Therefore we take $$x$$ and $$\theta$$ as parameters and regard Equations 3 as parametric equations of $$S$$ . The parameter domain is given by $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .

example.paragraph: Find parametric equations for the surface generated by rotating the curve $$y = \sin x$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis. Use these equations to graph the surface of revolution.

$${x = x} {y = \sin x\cos\theta} {z = \sin x\sin\theta}$$
and the parameter domain is $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using a computer to plot these equations, we obtain the graph in Figure 13.

section.paragraph: We can adapt Equations 3 to represent a surface obtained through revolution about the $$y$$ - or $$z$$ -axis (see Exercise 30).
section.heading: Tangent Planes
section.paragraph: We now find the tangent plane to a parametric surface $$S$$ traced out by a vector function
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

at a point $$P_{0}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ . If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a grid curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 14.) The tangent vector to $$C_{1}$$ at $$P_{0}$$ is obtained by taking the partial derivative of $$\mathbf{r}$$ with respect to $$\upsilon$$ :

$$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{k}$$

Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a grid curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ , and its tangent vector at $$P_{0}$$ is

$$\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{k}$$

If $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is not $$0$$ , then the surface $$S$$ is called smooth (it has no “corners”). For a smooth surface, the tangent plane is the plane that contains the tangent vectors $$\mathbf{r}_{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ , and the vector $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is a normal vector to the tangent plane.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Find the tangent plane to the surface with parametric equations $$x = u^{2}$$ , $$y = \upsilon^{2}$$ , $$z = u + 2\upsilon$$ at the point $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ .
Solution We first compute the tangent vectors:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\mathbf{k} = 2u\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{k}} \\ {\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{k} = 2\upsilon\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
Thus a normal vector to the tangent plane is

$$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {2u} & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & {2v} & 2 \end{matrix} \right| = - 2v\mathbf{i} - 4u\mathbf{j} + 4\mathit{uv}\mathbf{k}$$
Notice that the point $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ corresponds to the parameter values $$u = 1$$ and $$\upsilon = 1$$ , so the normal vector there is
$$- 2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}$$
Therefore an equation of the tangent plane at $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ is
$$- 2\left( {x - 1} \right) - 4\left( {y - 1} \right) + 4\left( {z - 3} \right) = 0$$

section.heading: Surface Area
section.paragraph: Now we define the surface area of a general parametric surface given by Equation 1. For simplicity we start by considering a surface $$S$$ whose parameter domain $$D$$ is a rectangle, and we divide it into subrectangles $$R_{ij}$$ . Let’s choose $$({u_{i}^{*},\upsilon_{j}^{*}})$$ to be the lower left corner of $$R_{ij}$$ . (See Figure 16.)

One of the squares in the grid is shaded and labeled R_(i j). The bottom side of the square is labeled Delta u and the right side is labeled Delta v. A horizontal arrow, labeled r, points rightward from the first part to the second part. In the second part, the rectangular grid from the first part is transformed into a curved surface with grid lines. The curved rectangular surface has its shorter sides parallel to the x z plane and the x y plane and the longer sides parallel to the y z plane and x y plane. The rectangle is tilted to the right and bulges outward to the front and slightly to the right. The same rectangle which was shaded in the first part is shaded in the second part as well and labeled S_(i j). A point marked near the bottom left corner of the square is labeled P(i j).

figure.caption: The image of the subrectangle $$R_{ij}$$ is the patch $$S_{ij}$$ .

section.paragraph: The part $$S_{ij}$$ of the surface $$S$$ that corresponds to $$R_{ij}$$ is called a patch and has the point $$P_{ij}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}{({u_{i}^{*},v_{j}^{*}})}$$ as one of its corners. Let
and
$$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}^{*} = \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}{({u_{i}^{*},v_{j}^{*}})}$$
be the tangent vectors at $$P_{ij}$$ as given by Equations 5 and 4.

Figure 17(a) shows how the two edges of the patch that meet at $$P_{ij}$$ can be approximated by vectors. These vectors, in turn, can be approximated by the vectors $$\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}$$ because partial derivatives can be approximated by difference quotients. So we approximate $$S_{ij}$$ by the parallelogram determined by the vectors $$\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}$$ . This parallelogram is shown in Figure 17(b) and lies in the tangent plane to $$S$$ at $$P_{ij}$$ . The area of this parallelogram is

$$\left| {\left( {\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}} \right) \times \left( {\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right)} \right| = \left| {\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right|\Delta u\Delta\upsilon$$
and so an approximation to the area of $$S$$ is
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right|\Delta u\Delta\upsilon}}$$

Our intuition tells us that this approximation gets better as we increase the number of subrectangles, and we recognize the double sum as a Riemann sum for the double integral $$\iint_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}} \right|dud\upsilon}$$ . This motivates the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If a smooth parametric surface $$S$$ is given by the equation
and $$S$$ is covered just once as $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ ranges throughout the parameter domain $$D$$ , then the surface area of $$S$$ is

$${\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\mathbf{k}} {\mathbf{r}_{v} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\mathbf{k}}$$

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius $$a$$ .
Solution In Example 4 we found the parametric representation
$${x = a\sin\phi\cos\theta} {y = a\sin\phi\sin\theta} {z = a\cos\phi}$$
where the parameter domain is
$$D = \left\{ (\phi,\theta) \middle| 0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi \right\}$$
We first compute the cross product of the tangent vectors:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial\phi} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\phi} & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\phi} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta} & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta} \end{matrix} \right| = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {a\cos\phi\cos\theta} & {a\cos\phi\sin\theta} & {- a\sin\phi} \\ {- a\sin\phi\sin\theta} & {a\sin\phi\cos\theta} & 0 \end{matrix} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}}{= a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$
Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right| = \sqrt{a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi{\cos}^{2}\theta + a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi{\sin}^{2}\theta + a^{4}{\sin}^{2}\phi{\cos}^{2}\phi^{}}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {r_{\phi} \times r_{\theta}} \right|}{= \sqrt{a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi + a^{4}{\sin}^{2}\phi{\cos}^{2}\phi^{}} = a^{2}\sqrt{{\sin}^{2}\phi^{}} = a^{2}\sin\phi}} \end{array}$$
since $$\sin\phi \geqslant 0$$ for $$0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi$$ . Therefore, by Definition 6, the area of the sphere is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right|dA = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{a^{2}\sin\phi d\phi d\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= a^{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin\phi d\phi = a^{2}\left( {2\pi} \right)2 = 4\pi a^{2}}}}}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Surface Area of the Graph of a Function
section.paragraph: For the special case of a surface $$S$$ with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lies in $$D$$ and $$f$$ has continuous partial derivatives, we take $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters. The parametric equations are
$${x = x} {y = y} {z = f\left( {x,y} \right)}$$
so
$${\mathbf{r}_{x} = \mathbf{i} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right)\mathbf{k}} {\mathbf{r}_{y} = \mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right)\mathbf{k}}$$
and

$$\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \end{matrix} \right| = - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$
Thus we have

$$|\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y}| = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right)^{2} + 1} = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}$$
and the surface area formula in Definition 6 becomes
$$A(S) = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}$$
Notice the similarity between the surface area formula in Equation 9 and the arc length formula
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}}dx$$
from Section 8.1.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Find the area of the part of the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ that lies under the plane $$z = 9$$ .

Solution The plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ , $$z = 9$$ . Therefore the given surface lies above the disk $$D$$ with center the origin and radius $$3$$ . (See Figure 18.) Using Formula 9, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( {2x} \right)^{2} + \left( {2y} \right)^{2}}dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + 4{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dA}}}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: The question remains whether our definition of surface area (6) is consistent with the surface area formula from single-variable calculus (8.2.4).

We consider the surface $$S$$ obtained by rotating the curve $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis, where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ is continuous. From Equations 3 we know that parametric equations of $$S$$ are
$$x = x y = f(x)\cos\theta z = f(x)\sin\theta a \leqslant x \leqslant b 0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$
To compute the surface area of $$S$$ we need the tangent vectors

$$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{r}_{x} & = & {\mathbf{i} + f^{\prime}(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{j} + f^{\prime}(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{k}} \\ \mathbf{r}_{\theta} & = & {- f(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + f(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & {f^{\prime}(x)\cos\theta} & {f^{\prime}(x)\sin\theta} \\ 0 & {- f(x)\sin\theta} & {f(x)\cos\theta} \end{matrix} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}}{= f(x)f^{\prime}(x)\mathbf{i} - f(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{j} - f(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$
and so

$$\begin{array}{l} {|\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}| = \sqrt{{\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}{\lbrack f^{\prime}(x)\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta + {\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\left| r_{x} \times r_{\theta} \right|} = \sqrt{\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}\left\lbrack {1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right\rbrack^{}} = f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} \end{array}$$
because $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ . Therefore the area of $$S$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right|_{}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}dxd\theta}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= 2\pi{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}dx}}}} \end{array}$$
This is precisely the formula that was used to define the area of a surface of revolution in single-variable calculus (8.2.4).
